Something is representational when it stands for, depicts, or points to something beyond itself — something real that exists outside the thing doing the depicting.

A representational thing is essentially a stand-in or a depiction. It is not the real thing; it represents the real thing.
In Art — the most common use

This is where you will encounter the word most often.

A representational artwork — a painting, drawing, or sculpture — depicts something from the real world in a recognizable way. When you look at it, you can clearly tell what it is showing. It is representing reality.

  • A portrait of a person → representational
  • A painting of fruit on a table → representational
  • A landscape of mountains → representational

The opposite of representational art is abstract art. Abstract art does not try to show any recognizable real-world subject. It uses shapes, colors, and forms that don't clearly look like anything specific. A Jackson Pollock canvas covered in splattered paint has no recognizable subject — it is abstract, not representational.

There is also a middle ground: semi-representational (or semi-abstract) art, where you can vaguely recognize a subject, but it has been heavily distorted or simplified. Many Cubist paintings by Picasso work this way — you can make out a face, but it is broken and rearranged into geometric fragments.

The key diagnostic question for art is: Does this work try to show something real and recognizable from the world? If yes — representational. If no — abstract.

Here, representational describes a system where a person or group acts on behalf of a larger group.

In a representational democracy (you may also hear "representative democracy"), citizens do not vote directly on every law or decision. Instead, they elect people to represent their interests — to speak, debate, and vote in their name. Those elected officials represent the people.

A parliament or congress is a representational body because it is composed of individuals who each stand in for a portion of the population. Their role is to represent, not to act purely for themselves.

The core question here: Does this person or institution act in the name of, and on behalf of, a larger group? If yes — representational.

Beyond art and politics, representational simply means functioning as a representation of something else — being a depiction, a symbol, or a model that communicates something about another thing.

  • A map is representational — it represents real terrain
  • A diagram of a molecule is representational — it depicts a structure you cannot see with the naked eye
  • A scale model of a building is representational — it shows what the full building looks like
  • A bar chart is representational — it visually represents numerical data
  • A flag is representational — it represents a nation or cause

In every case, the thing itself is not the real thing — it stands in for the real thing and conveys information about it.
In Philosophy and Cognitive Science (a more technical context)

Philosophers use representational to describe mental states that are about something in the world.

Your beliefs, thoughts, and perceptions are called representational because they point outward — they represent things outside your mind. When you believe "there is a cup on the table," that belief represents a state of the real world. It is a mental picture of something external.

This is distinct from mental states that are purely internal and not about anything in particular, like a vague feeling of restlessness with no identifiable cause. A thought that is about something — that depicts or refers to something — is representational.
The single thread connecting all uses

Across every context, the meaning is consistent:

Something is representational when it depicts, stands for, symbolizes, or acts in place of something else — particularly something real.

If a thing represents something, we describe it as representational. It is simply the adjective form of the verb "represent."
A memorable contrast to lock it in

Imagine two paintings hanging side by side.

The first is a detailed, realistic painting of a red apple on a white cloth. You can see the shine, the stem, the shadow beneath it. That painting is representational — it represents a real object from the world.

The second is a canvas of bold red and white shapes that swirl and overlap, beautiful but deliberately not showing anything specific. No apple, no object, no scene you can name. That painting is abstract — not representational.

That contrast — between depicting something real and recognizable versus not depicting anything specific — is the beating heart of what "representational" means. Everything else across art, politics, philosophy, and general language is a variation on that same idea: representational things point beyond themselves to something they stand in for.
